--- title: "K-Means Clustering from Scratch" author: "Tweety Chang" date: 2025-06-06 date-format: "MMMM YYYY" description: "K-Means built from scratch, validated against scikit-learn, and improved by feature scaling: agreement with species rises from 0.63 to 0.88 (adjusted Rand)." categories: [Machine Learning, Segmentation] image: figures/fig6_kmeans_k3.png callout-appearance: minimal --- ::: {.biz-value} ### Results - **Question:** Can two body measurements separate penguin species without using the labels, and how should the number of clusters be chosen? - **Approach:** Wrote K-Means from scratch, validated it against scikit-learn, and compared k = 2–7 with WCSS and silhouette scores. - **Key finding:** Feature scaling mattered more than the algorithm. Standardizing the two measurements raised agreement with the true species from **0.63 to 0.88** (adjusted Rand index) and recovered Chinstrap penguins as their own cluster. - **Judgment:** Silhouette slightly prefers k = 2. k = 3 is chosen because, once features are scaled, it costs little separation and matches a real three-group structure. Species labels never enter the fitting. ::: ## The Question Clustering looks for structure when there is no target variable. This project asks whether two measurements, **bill length** and **flipper length**, are enough to separate the three penguin species in the [Palmer Penguins](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/) data without seeing the labels. The labels are used only afterwards, to grade the result. Segmenting customers or borrowers raises the same questions as this project: which features to use, how to scale them, and how many groups the data actually supports. ## Data The dataset has 333 penguins with complete measurements: 146 Adélie, 68 Chinstrap, and 119 Gentoo. Clustering uses only `bill_length_mm` and `flipper_length_mm`. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Data preview (first 5 rows)"} | species | island | bill_length_mm | bill_depth_mm | flipper_length_mm | body_mass_g | sex | year | |----------|------------|----------------|---------------|-------------------|-------------|--------|------| | Adelie | Torgersen | 39.1 | 18.7 | 181 | 3750 | male | 2007 | | Adelie | Torgersen | 39.5 | 17.4 | 186 | 3800 | female | 2007 | | Adelie | Torgersen | 40.3 | 18.0 | 195 | 3250 | female | 2007 | | Adelie | Torgersen | 36.7 | 19.3 | 193 | 3450 | female | 2007 | | Adelie | Torgersen | 39.3 | 20.6 | 190 | 3650 | male | 2007 | ::: ## K-Means From Scratch K-Means alternates two steps until assignments stop changing: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. Because the result depends on the random starting centroids, the implementation runs several restarts and keeps the solution with the lowest within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS). **Figure 1. Iteration 1:** random starting centroids, with overlapping groups. ![Custom K-Means, iteration 1](figures/fig_kmeans_iter1.png){#fig-kmeans-iter1} **Figure 2. Iteration 2:** one update moves centroids toward the dense regions, and most of the structure appears. ![Custom K-Means, iteration 2](figures/fig_kmeans_iter2.png){#fig-kmeans-iter2} **Figure 3. Converged solution:** centroid movement has stopped. ![Custom K-Means, converged](figures/fig_kmeans_iter10.png){#fig-kmeans-final} ### Validation against scikit-learn ::: {#58de6d7e .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
Custom (bill, flipper) scikit-learn (bill, flipper) Custom WCSS scikit-learn WCSS
Cluster 1 (38.45, 187.05) (38.45, 187.05) 13859.5 13858.9
Cluster 2 (45.95, 196.73) (45.95, 196.84)
Cluster 3 (47.63, 216.92) (47.65, 217.00)
``` ::: ::: With restarts, the custom implementation and scikit-learn reach the same solution. A single K-Means run can stop in a worse local optimum, which is why an earlier version of this analysis showed different centroids for the two implementations. ## Choosing k ::: {#ead28924 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](Key_Drivers_Analysis_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=720 height=298} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
WCSS (raw) Silhouette (raw) Silhouette (standardized)
k
2 20949.8 0.612 0.539
3 13858.9 0.480 0.519
4 9587.1 0.445 0.504
5 7423.0 0.425 0.433
6 6326.3 0.414 0.401
7 5257.1 0.431 0.410
``` ::: ::: The WCSS curve bends at k = 3, and silhouette is highest at k = 2. On raw features, the gap between k = 2 and k = 3 is large (0.612 vs. 0.480). After standardizing, it nearly disappears (0.539 vs. 0.519), so k = 3 gives up very little separation in exchange for a finer, more useful segmentation. ## Does Scaling Matter? Flipper length varies about 2.5 times as much as bill length (standard deviation 14.0 mm vs. 5.5 mm), so on raw data it dominates the distance calculation and bill length has little influence on the clusters. Standardizing gives both measurements equal weight. The labels are used here only to grade the clusters, never to fit them: ::: {#98906525 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Adjusted Rand index vs. species: raw 0.63, standardized 0.88 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Cluster 1 Cluster 2 Cluster 3
Raw features
Adelie 106 38 2
Chinstrap 9 54 5
Gentoo 0 2 117
``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Cluster 1 Cluster 2 Cluster 3
Standardized
Adelie 141 4 1
Chinstrap 5 59 4
Gentoo 0 1 118
``` ::: ::: - **Raw features:** Gentoo separates cleanly, but 54 of 68 Chinstrap penguins share a middle cluster with 38 Adélie penguins, so that cluster is not a single species. - **Standardized:** each cluster corresponds to one species, and 59 of 68 Chinstrap penguins are grouped together. Adjusted Rand index rises from 0.63 to 0.88. **Figure 4. Final raw-feature clustering (k = 3)** ![K-Means clustering result, k = 3](figures/fig6_kmeans_k3.png){#fig-kmeans-k3} ## Takeaways and Limitations - **Scale before you cluster.** With distance-based methods, the units of the inputs decide the result. Here, scaling changed the answer more than the choice of k did. - **Restart K-Means.** A single run can stop in a poor local optimum. Multiple restarts, or k-means++ initialization, should be the default. - **k is a judgment call.** The metrics narrow the choice; the purpose of the segmentation decides it. - **Limitations:** only two features are used, and K-Means assumes round, similar-sized clusters. Adding bill depth, or trying a Gaussian mixture model that allows elongated clusters, would be natural next steps.
